newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FOCUS-Australia's fifth rate cut surprises markets.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Australia's fifth rate cut surprises markets.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) took financial markets by surprise again on Wednesday, cutting official interest rates for the fifth time in a year.
The cut itself, which reduced the bank's official cash rate by half a percentage point to 5.0 percent, was widely expected following the release of inflation and wages data last week.
But most analysts had expected the bank to wait until after its next board meeting on August 5 before making its move.

"This change, like the four previous reductions in interest rates over the past year, is based on the improving picture for Australia's medium-term inflation performance, which opens up scope for faster growth and employment," the RBA said.

The government, burdened with an unemployment rate that appears stuck above 8.5 percent and slumping in the opinion polls, welcomed the central bank's announcement but economists said the timing caught the market off guard.
"The only oddity in the whole thing was the timing," said Michael Blythe, senior economist with the Commonwealth Bank.
Some economists said there may be room for yet another cut if the latest one fails to do the job.
"There might be some attempt to price in another rate cut," said Chris Caton, chief economist at Bankers Trust.
Tony Meer, economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said the bank's comment that the economy had room to grow in the next two to three years without threatening inflation was significant.
"It suggests the bank sees enough room for yet another easing, if not two," Meer said.
The RBA noted that underlying inflation in the year to June was 1.7 percent and that it expected underlying inflation to stay below two percent into 1998.
Underlying inflation strips out volatile elements of the consumer price index, such as mortgage rates.
The bank said economic growth in 1997 had been picking up, but that it remained moderate. Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew at an annual rate of 2.4 percent in the March quarter.
"The crucial test for monetary policy is to have the setting that will best contribute to low inflation and economic growth in the long run," the RBA said.
"...Monetary policy should not stand in the way of a period of stronger growth that can be accommodated without breaching the inflation objective," the bank said.

The RBA said that although earlier rate cuts were still working their way through the economy, it believed the latest cut would not fuel inflation. "The balance of risks at this time is such as to favour this further easing of monetary policy."
Treasurer Peter Costello said the Australian economy was in a strong position after the rate cut, which he said reflected the government's policy of keeping interest rates low.
"This is a conjunction of very significant economic news which sets Australia up for a very good outlook over the forthcoming year," Costello said.
The Australian dollar dropped half a U.S. cent to US$0.7395 on the news at 2330 GMT, but bounced back to close a full cent higher at US$0.7462/67 -- its best local close in three weeks.
Bonds rallied on the news but gains were quickly pared back and the 10-year government bond finished modestly lower at 6.51.
Dealers said the rate cut had been factored in and the rally evaporated as the market pondered another rate cut.

"A confident central bank, a resilient Australian dollar and only moderate growth response to current low rates, all point to a further reduction over the next quarter," said Westpac Banking Corp economist Bill Evans.
The All Ordinaries share index closed 3.1 points up at 2,735 as sellers took profits after a small rate cut rally.
